zh.title: 之七 · 一眼看得全
zh.deck: 一路问过去，和画一张一眼看得全的图，不是同一种次序。

paragraphs: 有人第一次去朋友家，是一路问过去的：到路口问一次，过了桥再问一次。后来他给别人画去那儿的路，没照自己问的次序画，画了一张图，一眼看得全。
第四部分讲人的奴役，末尾有一篇附录。开头的话是他自己说的：这一部分里我讲的正当的生活之道，不是排成一眼看得全的样子，是我照一条从另一条推起来方便，零零散散证明出来的。所以我打算在这里重新收拢一遍，归成几个要点。
第三部分末尾，他也回头把情感的定义重说过一遍，那一回说的是有几处要注意。这一回说的是次序：推起来方便的次序，一眼看不全。

sections.heading: 三十二章
paragraphs: 要点归成三十二章。第一章说，我们的一切努力，或者说欲望，都出于我们本性的必然；第三十二章说，人的力量很有限。中间讲人和人：和睦，友谊，谄媚，羞耻；也讲婚姻，钱，吃的，讲怎样对待穷人。
有几章注明请人去看前面哪一条附释。注出来的号码前后跳着：第十五章指第三十七，四十六，七十三条命题的附释，第十八章指第七十，七十一条，第二十二章指第五十七条，第二十五章又回到第三十七条。
许多章能在前面的正文里找到出处或者主干；也有几处把问题说得更具体：第十七章说，照顾穷人是整个社会的事；第二十章讲婚姻怎样才合乎理性。

sections.heading: 我们
paragraphs: 附录开头那两句里，他说我讲的，我证明的，我打算。到了三十二章的正文里，反复出现的则是我们。
第三十一章还留着一句显眼的我的：除了嫉妒的人，没有谁拿我的无力和不幸取乐。这话出自第四十五条命题的附释。附释里，它前面紧挨着一句：这是我的理由，我也就这样说服了自己。到了第三十一章，前面那一句换成了：正如我们已经说过的。

sections.heading: 收束
paragraphs: 第三十二章先说，人的力量很有限，外面的原因的力量无限地胜过它。可那些违背我们利益的事，我们要是知道自己尽了本分，知道我们的力量够不到躲开它们，知道我们是整个自然的一部分，跟着它的秩序走，就会平心承受。这一点要是清楚明白地懂了，我们身上用理解来界定的那一部分，也就是更好的那一部分，会在这里头安下心来。这一章的结尾是：
只要我们把这些理解对了，我们更好的那一部分的努力，就跟整个自然的秩序相合。

notes: 对应第四部分附录，尤其第15、17、18、20、22、25、31、32章，并对照第四十五条命题附释。正文保留可以跟读的回指与措辞变化。
不把三十二章硬分成已经全面查清的三十旧、二新；贫困与婚姻两处保留为具体展开，不宣称它们穷尽了一切新增。人称动词的精确统计也不作为本篇依据。
zh.aside: 《SAE第一批判》书末的术语表，开头交代：本表是本书五章正文的汇编，不新增判决；释义跟正文冲突的地方，以正文为准；每一条后面括注出处。斯宾诺莎的三十二章里，也有几章注明请人去看前面哪一条附释。这是旁注，不是论证。

en.title: A View of the Whole
en.deck: The easiest order for proving something may not be the easiest order for seeing how to live.

paragraphs: On a first visit to a friend’s house, you ask directions at one junction, then ask again after the bridge. Later, drawing a route for someone else, you do not reproduce the sequence of your questions. You make a map they can take in at once.

Part IV of the Ethics ends with an appendix. Spinoza explains why it is needed. His account of right living has not been arranged for an easy view of the whole. He proved its elements here and there, in the order that made deduction convenient. Now he wants to gather them into main points.

At the end of Part III he had restated definitions because there were matters to notice. Here the difficulty is the arrangement. What works for moving from one proof to the next may not show the reader the overall shape.

sections.heading: Thirty-two chapters
paragraphs: The appendix gathers its points into thirty-two short chapters. The first relates our striving and desires to the necessity of our nature. The last returns to the limits of human power.
Between them come relations with other people: concord, friendship, flattery, shame, marriage, money, food and the care of the poor. The subjects of daily life occupy the summary of a deductive work.

Some chapters direct us to earlier scholia, but the references do not proceed neatly in order. Chapter Fifteen points to the scholia of Propositions Thirty-Seven, Forty-Six and Seventy-Three; Eighteen to Seventy and Seventy-One; Twenty-Two returns to Fifty-Seven; Twenty-Five to Thirty-Seven again.

Much of the appendix gathers earlier material. Other passages make matters newly concrete: Chapter Seventeen assigns care of the poor to society as a whole; Chapter Twenty asks when marriage accords with reason. These are not merely new headings placed over a copied sequence of proofs.

sections.heading: From “I” to “we”
paragraphs: In the introductory sentences Spinoza speaks of what I have said, what I have demonstrated, what I intend to gather. The short chapters themselves move repeatedly into “we.”
Chapter Thirty-One preserves a striking “my”: nobody but an envious person takes pleasure in my weakness and misfortune. It recalls the scholium to Proposition Forty-Five.

In that scholium, the sentence follows a personal declaration: this is my reason, and this is how I have persuaded myself. In the appendix, the lead-in is instead a backward-looking “as we have said.”
The claim is gathered into a collective summary. The small possessive remains, but its approach has changed.

sections.heading: At the end
paragraphs: Chapter Thirty-Two begins with our limited power. External causes surpass it immeasurably. Yet we can bear what goes against our interests more calmly if we know we have done what we could, that avoiding it lay beyond our power, and that we are parts of nature following its order.
If we understand this clearly and distinctly, the part of us defined by understanding—our better part—can find rest in that recognition.
The chapter closes by bringing that part’s striving into agreement with the order of the whole of nature, insofar as these things are rightly understood.
The map is not a promise that every obstacle disappears. It lets us see together what the scattered route was leading through.

en.aside: The glossary at the end of the SAE First Critique describes itself as a gathering of material from the preceding chapters, not a source of new verdicts; it provides locations and gives the main text priority if a formulation conflicts. Spinoza’s appendix also gathers and points backwards. That shared editorial act does not imply identical standards of authority.
notes: Locations: Part IV, Appendix, especially Chapters 15, 17, 18, 20, 22, 25, 31 and 32; compare IV.45, Scholium. The text’s backward references can be followed directly.

No exhaustive thirty-to-two division between old and new matter is claimed. The readings of poverty and marriage are identified as concrete emphases, not certified as the only topics absent from earlier argument. Exact grammatical-person totals are likewise omitted.
